title: Generative AI in Sociology
text:
The question behind the course
Large language models can classify text, suggest interpretations, generate treatments, conduct interviews, imitate survey respondents, take part in simulations, search for evidence and write code. None of those abilities tells us, on its own, whether a sociological claim is warranted. That is the problem this course takes seriously.
The course is about 60 per cent method and 40 per cent substantive sociology of AI. We use LLMs as research tools, but also study the social assumptions, institutions and inequalities that become visible through them. The aim is not to turn sociologists into software engineers. It is to make the technical steps understandable enough that you can decide what the output means, what it does not mean, and what should be checked next.
No prior programming course is required. We introduce Python gradually through actual research tasks. Each example names its input, shows the operation, displays the output and then asks what evidence would validate the resulting claim. You will be expected to explain the code in plain language. Remembering package syntax is much less important than understanding what a value represents and how it changes.

title: Generative AI in Sociology
text: What inference is the researcher trying to make, and what evidence would validate the use of an LLM for that inference?

title: Generative AI in Sociology
text:
Four parts of the semester

Evidence, measurement and interpretation (Weeks 1–4). We begin with research records, text annotation, qualitative analysis and multimodal observation.
Experiments and research encounters (Weeks 5–6). We examine generated treatments and interviews in which the next question depends on the preceding answer.
Synthetic populations and social simulation (Weeks 7–10). We ask what model-generated respondents and interacting agents can represent.
Research agents, replication and model audits (Weeks 11–14). We examine long-horizon research systems, reproducibility and LLMs as objects of sociological study.

The final project returns to the opening question. You will propose an LLM-related sociological study and show that its claims, data, model operations and validation plan fit together.

title: Generative AI in Sociology
text:
What this book contains
Each week is divided into two pages. The first gives you the sociological question, the readings and why they matter, the methodological background and the lecture slides. A separate Python page then gives you the worked input-to-output trace, complete workbook and take-home completion task. Week 14 is reserved for presentations and therefore has no Python page. The HTML edition is the canonical version: it is searchable and contains the live slide decks and downloads. The PDF is provided for reading and annotation away from the site.

title: Course structure and schedule
text:
A typical week
The seminar meets on Wednesdays from 9:30 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. The sequence is cumulative, but it is not a ladder of model capability. Each week introduces a different kind of sociological claim and asks what an LLM changes in the production of evidence.
Before class, read the essential material with the chapter question in mind. The additional readings are routes into a debate, not an undifferentiated list.
The normal 165-minute meeting has three clearly different parts:
The exact timing can move slightly when discussion is especially productive, but the middle of the class is reserved for collective discussion and the final part is reserved for working through the code together.
The coding strand teaches Python through actual LLM routines. Week 1 introduces values, strings and the anatomy of a call. From Week 2, students send a prompt to a model through OpenRouter or a supported local runtime. Later weeks add message lists, structured outputs, parsing, generation parameters, loops and, only after those are familiar, small functions with explicit parameters. Cached responses remain available when a service is unavailable, but they are the contingency rather than the main route.

Workbooks and code
The course assumes no prior Python knowledge. Each week has a separate Python work page immediately after its readings-and-slides page in the book navigation. Every required coding exercise is printed there in full. The code is divided into short blocks, and each block includes its exact input, a line-by-line explanation, the expected output and the research meaning of that output. This keeps the main weekly page focused on the readings and lecture while giving the code enough space to be explained properly.
The downloadable .py task file repeats the Python-page exercise exactly and provides a convenient place to run it. It does not contain an extra or more difficult assignment. The notebook is optional and provides further examples. Neither download substitutes for the explanation on the Python page. For every required block, be able to answer five questions:

What value enters, and what does it represent?
What is its Python type?
What operation is performed?
What value comes out?
What sociological claim could that output support, and what would still need checking?

Weeks 1–2 send the same synthetic or public teaching material through OpenRouter and Ollama. Students choose either route in Weeks 3–7 and compare both again in Week 8. A clearly labelled recorded return is supplied as a contingency if the hosted service, network or local runtime is unavailable; using that contingency does not reduce the completion mark.
Each developed week also has an Open in Google Colab link. Colab opens the notebook in a browser and supplies a temporary Python environment. Run the first setup cell once: it downloads the public cjbarrie/GenAI_Soc2026 repository and moves to the correct weekly folder so that the notebook can find its accompanying data. To keep your changes, use Colab’s File → Save a copy in Drive; the temporary runtime itself is not permanent. Colab uses the OpenRouter route because it cannot normally connect to Ollama running on your own computer.

title: Setting up Python, OpenRouter and Ollama
text:
Six pieces of the setup
The course uses real model calls from Week 1. Everyone configures both supported routes during the first two weeks. After that, you normally choose either OpenRouter or Ollama; Week 8 returns to a direct comparison.
This chapter separates several things that are easy to conflate: Python, a notebook, an SDK, an API, a server and a model. They work together, but they are not interchangeable names for the same thing.
Installing openrouter or ollama does not install Python, Jupyter or—in the OpenRouter case—the model. The packages are relatively small pieces of client software. Their job is to connect our Python code to a service.

title: Setting up Python, OpenRouter and Ollama
text:
What OpenRouter is
OpenRouter is a hosted routing service. We send one request to OpenRouter’s API and name a model using a string such as "openai/gpt-5.2". OpenRouter then selects an available provider endpoint for that model, forwards the request and returns the result. The model name and the provider that actually serves a request are therefore related but distinct pieces of the research record.
The course uses OpenRouter because one SDK and one key let us work with hosted models without learning a different provider library for every model. That convenience does not remove the need to record routing information, cost, data policy or the resolved model/provider when the service supplies it.

What happens during an OpenRouter call

Python stores the prompt and messages in memory on the student’s computer.
The openrouter SDK turns those Python objects into an HTTPS request.
The key is sent in an authorization header. It tells OpenRouter which account may make the request; it is not part of the prompt.
The request leaves the computer and reaches OpenRouter.
OpenRouter routes it to a provider serving the requested model.
The provider runs the model and sends a response back through OpenRouter.
The SDK turns the response into a Python object such as hosted_response.
Our code retrieves the returned message text from that object.

The network path is:
notebook → openrouter SDK → internet → OpenRouter → model provider
notebook ← Python response object ← internet ← OpenRouter ← model provider
The official OpenRouter SDK is a thin client for its REST API: it handles authentication, validates request fields and provides typed response objects. See the OpenRouter Python SDK and provider-routing documentation.
crumbs: 5  Setting up Python, OpenRouter and Ollama

title: Setting up Python, OpenRouter and Ollama
text:
What Ollama is
Ollama is an application and local model server. ollama pull ... downloads a named model artifact. When Ollama is running, it normally serves an API at http://localhost:11434/api. localhost means this same computer; it is not a website elsewhere on the internet.
The Python package named ollama is the client. It sends a request to the Ollama server. The server loads the requested model onto the available CPU/GPU and memory, runs inference and returns a response. No OpenRouter key is needed for this local API. Model download is a separate earlier network operation.

What happens during an Ollama call

Python stores the same prompt and messages in memory.
The ollama package turns those Python objects into an HTTP request.
The request goes to the Ollama server at localhost, normally on port 11434.
Ollama finds the downloaded model named by LOCAL_MODEL.
Ollama loads or reuses the model and performs inference on the computer.
Ollama returns JSON to the Python client.
The client gives us a Python response object such as local_response.
Our code retrieves the returned message text from that object.

The local path is:
notebook → ollama Python client → localhost:11434 → downloaded model
notebook ← Python response object ← localhost:11434 ← downloaded model
The local server normally requires no authentication because it listens on the same machine. Do not expose it to a network for this course. See Ollama’s official API introduction, chat endpoint and Python client.

title: Setting up Python, OpenRouter and Ollama
text:
What is actually sent?
An API request has a destination, headers and a body. The SDK handles the HTTP details, but the body is built from values we can inspect. A simplified hosted request body looks like this:
import json

hosted_request_body = {
    "model": "openai/gpt-5.2",
    "messages": [
        {"role": "user", "content": "Score this statement from 0 to 2."}
    ],
    "temperature": 0,
}

print(json.dumps(hosted_request_body, indent=2))
Python first holds a dictionary containing a string, a list, another dictionary and an integer. The SDK serializes that structure as JSON and sends it to the API. JSON is a text format for exchanging structured data; it is not the model itself.
The key belongs in the authorization header rather than in this body. That is why it should never be concatenated into the prompt or saved in the research material. The response travels back as JSON, and the SDK converts it into a typed response object.
The Ollama request has the same broad pieces but a local destination and route-specific options:
local_request_body = {
    "model": "gemma4:e2b-it-qat",
    "messages": hosted_request_body["messages"],
    "options": {"temperature": 0},
}

print(json.dumps(local_request_body, indent=2))
The model string, message list and settings are data supplied to the server. client.chat.send(...) and ollama.chat(...) are Python calls that perform the transport and return an object. Keeping these layers separate makes both debugging and methodological reporting easier.

Check the Ollama server before opening Python

ollama --version

curl http://localhost:11434/api/version

ollama --version checks that the command-line application is installed.
ollama list asks the running service which model artifacts are available.
curl .../api/version sends a direct HTTP request to the local API. A small JSON reply means the server is reachable.

import os
from getpass import getpass

if not os.getenv("OPENROUTER_API_KEY"):
    os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"] = getpass("OpenRouter course key (hidden): ")

title: Setting up Python, OpenRouter and Ollama
section: The same research request through both routes
text:
The same research request through both routes
Both calls begin with the same Python list:
text = "Most people can be trusted."
instruction = "Score the statement for generalized social trust from 0 to 2. Return one integer."
prompt = instruction + "\n\nStatement: " + text
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
text, instruction and prompt are strings. messages is a list containing one dictionary. The list is the input supplied to both SDKs.
The list and dictionary are not special LLM syntax. They are ordinary Python objects arranged in the form expected by the APIs. This is where the course begins teaching Python: first we construct a real model request; after the two calls, we inspect the objects we just used.

OpenRouter
from openrouter import OpenRouter

HOSTED_MODEL = "openai/gpt-5.2"

with OpenRouter(api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]) as client:
    hosted_response = client.chat.send(
        model=HOSTED_MODEL,
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0,
    )

hosted_choice = hosted_response.choices[0]
hosted_message = hosted_choice.message
hosted_answer = hosted_message.content.strip()
print(hosted_answer)
The call sends messages to a hosted model. The three following assignments unpack the first returned choice, its message and its text. They are kept separate in Weeks 1–2 so the response path is visible.


Ollama
import ollama

LOCAL_MODEL = "gemma4:e2b-it-qat"

local_response = ollama.chat(
    think=False,
    model=LOCAL_MODEL,
    messages=messages,
    options={"temperature": 0},
)

local_message = local_response.message
local_answer = local_message.content.strip()
print(local_answer)
Ollama receives the same message list, but inference runs on the local server. think=False asks the course model to return the requested answer directly; otherwise a short output allowance can be consumed by a separate reasoning field before visible answer text is produced. Its generation settings are placed inside options, and its response text is reached through response.message.content.

title: Setting up Python, OpenRouter and Ollama
section: Use the model routine to learn Python objects
text:
Use the model routine to learn Python objects
After both calls have run, Week 1 pauses to inspect what Python now holds:
first_message = messages[0]
routes_match = hosted_answer == local_answer
hosted_character_count = len(hosted_answer)

print(type(text))                    # str
print(type(messages))                # list
print(type(first_message))           # dict
print(type(hosted_character_count))  # int
print(type(routes_match))            # bool
These types have immediate roles in the model routine:

a string stores text, including the prompt, model name and returned answer;
a list stores ordered items, such as conversation messages or returned choices;
a dictionary stores named fields, such as role and content;
an integer stores a whole-number quantity, such as a character count;
a Boolean stores True or False, such as whether two returned strings match.

The SDK also returns objects defined by its own package. We often retrieve their fields with dot notation:
hosted_choices = hosted_response.choices
hosted_message = hosted_choices[0].message
hosted_answer = hosted_message.content

local_message = local_response.message
local_answer = local_message.content
Compare three ways of retrieving something:
messages[0]                    # position 0 in a list
first_message["content"]      # field named "content" in a dictionary
hosted_message.content         # attribute named content on an SDK object
The square brackets do two different jobs because the object on their left differs. A list uses a numeric position. A dictionary uses a key. Dot notation retrieves an attribute supplied by the SDK’s response class. We inspect the object with type(...) before assuming how to access it.

title: AI use: permitted with responsibility and disclosure
text:
There are a large number of competing policies when it comes to AI. Here is just a selection of several hundred from colleges in the United States: AI policies across universities. You will find that they all differ—sometimes drastically. This is a reasonable, though selective, representation of where we stand at this moment in academia. Some will say you cannot use AI; others will say you cannot do without it. I am sure I would agree with elements of what both sides are saying. In fact, that is basically where I stand.
I will flesh this out with you in Week 1, but here is the thing: you are graduate students at one of the top Sociology programmes in the world. To excel in this field, you will need to understand the field. You will need to think hard—sometimes until your head is spinning. You will need to work hard—it is only this way that you really understand something. Or you could rely 100% of the time on some commercial language model to do the hard work for you. If you do that, you will notice that the muscles you require to operate in this world fail to develop. You will notice that others around you are able to speak about the social world and research design with a fluency you have not developed.
I am not here to discipline and punish. I am not interested in doing so. I think language models and modern-day AI software are some of the most exciting technologies around. We can use them to conduct research at a pace and scale previously not possible. But we can also use them as a substitute for thinking. So ask yourself: am I using this as a tool to augment my learning and enhance my research? Or am I using this as a substitute for myself? Only you can answer that question.
Use of generative AI is permitted in this course, with responsibility and disclosure. If AI materially assists submitted work, include a brief note naming the tool or model, explaining what you used it for, what you incorporated, and how you checked it. When an LLM is itself part of the research method, prompts, outputs, settings, dates, provider or local runtime, and validation decisions belong in the research record. You remain responsible for every claim and every line of code you submit.
Finally, the assignments for this course are principally based on class work and explanation. We will go through notebooks together, check one another’s work, and ask you to explain code in full. The individual oral code walkthrough requires you to explain the code yourself without live AI assistance. title: Week 1 — What kind of research technology is an LLM?
text:
Sociological and methodological background
Social scientists have always relied on research technologies: questionnaires, recording devices, codebooks, statistical packages and archives. Each makes some work easier while standardizing or hiding other decisions. LLMs extend that pattern. They can turn a natural-language instruction into a classification, summary, interview probe or simulated response, but the fluency of the return makes it unusually easy to forget the chain of decisions that produced it.
Reproducibility is therefore introduced at the beginning, not saved for the end. A model name may point to a changing service; a provider may route the same request to different infrastructure; a prompt may be edited without versioning; and a polished answer may be copied without its raw response. The Week 1 question is modest: can another researcher see what was asked, what answered and what you did next?

title: Week 1 — What kind of research technology is an LLM?
section: Synthesis of the current LLM literature
text:
Synthesis of the current LLM literature
The three essential readings make different kinds of claim. Davidson and Karell offer a broad methodological framework. Alvero and colleagues ask what generative AI means for sociology as a discipline. The course chapter inventories specific operations and argues that familiar standards must be reconsidered when the transformation is prompt-sensitive and the model is proprietary. Messeri and Crockett’s broader warning about an “illusion of understanding” is relevant here: faster production can encourage broader claims without improving the evidence underneath them. The practical response is not to reject the technology. It is to make the operation visible and keep validation separate from generation.

text:
Today’s routine: One statement → one shared prompt → two model calls → two research records.
Python introduced: notebook cells, strings, variables, functions we call, lists, dictionaries, indexing, SDK objects, attributes, methods, integers and Booleans.
Your change: replace the trust statement and run both routes again.



Load the course settings and SDKs
Run the notebook’s Prepare the notebook environment cell first. In Colab, that cell installs the two Python SDKs and sets IN_COLAB = True. Locally, it checks that Jupyter was started from the course environment; if packages are missing, close Jupyter and run uv sync followed by uv run jupyter lab from the repository root.
This next cell reads the two centrally recorded model names and asks for the hosted key without displaying it. Treat the key entry as setup; never include it in the recording.
import json
import os
from getpass import getpass
from pathlib import Path

try:
    import ollama
    from openrouter import OpenRouter
except ModuleNotFoundError as error:
    raise ModuleNotFoundError(
        "A course SDK is missing. Open a terminal in the complete GenAI_Soc2026 "
        "folder, run 'uv sync --frozen', then run this task with 'uv run python'."
    ) from error

ROOT = Path.cwd()
while not (ROOT / "config" / "course_models.json").exists() and ROOT != ROOT.parent:
    ROOT = ROOT.parent

if not (ROOT / "config" / "course_models.json").exists():
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "The complete GenAI_Soc2026 repository could not be found. A task or "
        "notebook downloaded by itself is not enough for local work. Open a terminal "
        "in the complete course folder and run this file from there."
    )

config = json.loads((ROOT / "config" / "course_models.json").read_text())
HOSTED_MODEL = config["hosted"]["model"]
LOCAL_MODEL = config["local"]["model"]

if not os.getenv("OPENROUTER_API_KEY"):
    os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"] = getpass("OpenRouter course key (hidden): ")

print("Hosted model:", HOSTED_MODEL)
print("Local model:", LOCAL_MODEL)






Read this setup cell



Input: installed Python packages, config/course_models.json, and—if it is not already set—the hidden OpenRouter key. Operations: import makes an installed tool available; Path.cwd() gives Python the current folder; the while block walks upward until it finds the course configuration; json.loads(...) turns the file’s JSON text into a dictionary; square brackets retrieve the two model names. Output: HOSTED_MODEL and LOCAL_MODEL are strings. getpass(...) accepts the key without echoing it. The folder-search code is supplied setup and is not assessed.




Store the research material and construct one shared message list
The research material begins as strings. The list named messages is the exact shared input to both SDKs.
text = "Most people can be trusted."
instruction = (
    "Score the statement for generalized social trust from 0 to 2. "
    "Return one integer."
)
prompt = instruction + "\n\nStatement: " + text
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]

print("text:", text)
print("type(text):", type(text))
print("messages:", messages)
print("type(messages):", type(messages))






Input and output



text and instruction are strings. + joins those strings with the labelled statement to create prompt; \n means start a new line. The braces create one dictionary with two named fields, and the brackets place that dictionary in a list called messages. Both clients will receive this same list. type(...) reports the kind of Python object without changing it.




Send the message list through OpenRouter and unpack its return
Inference occurs remotely. The response path is unpacked one object at a time before the returned text is printed.
with OpenRouter(api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]) as client:
    hosted_response = client.chat.send(
        model=HOSTED_MODEL,
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0,
    )

hosted_choice = hosted_response.choices[0]
hosted_message = hosted_choice.message
hosted_answer = hosted_message.content.strip()
print("OpenRouter raw text:", hosted_answer)






What the hosted call does



The call receives three named inputs: the hosted model string, the message list and temperature=0. with ... as client opens the SDK client and closes it after the indented call. The service returns a response object containing a list named choices; [0] selects the first choice. .message retrieves its message and .content retrieves the returned text. .strip() removes surrounding whitespace but does not change the score itself.




Send the same message list through Ollama and unpack its return
Inference occurs through the Ollama server on this computer. The same messages enter, but the call and response path differ.
if IN_COLAB:
    local_response = None
    local_message = None
    local_answer = None
    print("Ollama was not called: Colab cannot reach the local Ollama server.")
else:
    local_response = ollama.chat(think=False, 
        model=LOCAL_MODEL,
        messages=messages,
        options={"temperature": 0},
    )
    local_message = local_response.message
    local_answer = local_message.content.strip()
    print("Ollama raw text:", local_answer)






What the local call does



if IN_COLAB checks the Boolean created by the setup cell. In Colab, the three local values become None, Python’s marker for “no value,” and no local request is attempted. Locally, ollama.chat(think=False, ...) sends the same message list to the Ollama server on this computer. Ollama’s response shape differs: the message is available as .message, without a choices list. A local route changes where inference occurs; it does not validate the score.




Use the request to learn strings, lists and dictionaries
Both calls have now run. We can use the objects involved in those calls to learn Python rather than switching to an unrelated example.
first_message = messages[0]

print("text value:", text)
print("text type:", type(text))
print("messages value:", messages)
print("messages type:", type(messages))
print("number of messages:", len(messages))
print("first message:", first_message)
print("first message type:", type(first_message))
print("role field:", first_message["role"])
print("content field:", first_message["content"])






Read the objects from left to right



text is a string: one text value. messages is a list: an ordered collection whose first position is numbered 0. messages[0] therefore retrieves the first item and = assigns it to the new variable first_message. That item is a dictionary: a collection of named fields. first_message["role"] retrieves the value stored under the key "role"; first_message["content"] retrieves the actual prompt. len(messages) calls a built-in function and returns the integer 1. Parentheses contain the value passed to a function; commas separate multiple inputs. We call print, type and len, but students do not define a function until Week 9. None of these operations contacts a model. They inspect the input already held by Python.




Use the returns to learn objects, attributes and methods
The two SDKs returned objects defined by their packages. They are not plain strings, lists or dictionaries, even though they contain some of those types.
hosted_choices = hosted_response.choices

print("hosted response type:", type(hosted_response))
print("hosted choices type:", type(hosted_choices))
print("first hosted choice type:", type(hosted_choice))
print("hosted message type:", type(hosted_message))
print("hosted answer type:", type(hosted_answer))

print("local response type:", type(local_response))
print("local message type:", type(local_message))
print("local answer type:", type(local_answer))






Why some fields use dots and others use brackets



hosted_response.choices uses dot notation to retrieve an attribute supplied by the OpenRouter response class. Because choices is a list, [0] then retrieves its first item. .message and .content retrieve further attributes. By contrast, first_message["content"] uses a dictionary key. Finally, .strip() is a string method: it returns a new string without surrounding whitespace. A useful beginner question is therefore not simply “what does this line do?” but “what type of object is on the left of the dot or brackets?”




Derive an integer and a Boolean from the returned strings
hosted_character_count = len(hosted_answer)
local_character_count = None if local_answer is None else len(local_answer)
routes_match = None if local_answer is None else hosted_answer == local_answer

print("hosted character count:", hosted_character_count)
print("count type:", type(hosted_character_count))
print("routes returned identical text:", routes_match)
print("comparison type:", type(routes_match))






Two more built-in Python types



len(hosted_answer) counts the characters in a returned string and produces an integer. The short if ... else ... expression first checks whether an Ollama result exists. In Colab it returns None; locally, == compares the two strings and produces the Boolean True or False. None here means “not run,” not model disagreement. Identical returned strings would show agreement on this run, but would not show that either answer measures social trust validly.




Preserve the two runs as separate research records
Each dictionary keeps route, requested model, input and raw output together. This makes the comparison inspectable.
hosted_record = {
    "route": "openrouter",
    "model": HOSTED_MODEL,
    "input": text,
    "raw_output": hosted_answer,
}
local_record = {
    "route": "ollama",
    "model": LOCAL_MODEL,
    "input": text,
    "raw_output": local_answer,
}

research_records = [hosted_record, local_record]

print(hosted_record)
print(local_record)
print("record collection type:", type(research_records))
print("first recorded route:", research_records[0]["route"])

# ONE CHANGE: replace text with "You cannot be too careful in dealing with people."
# Then rerun every cell from the shared message list onward.






Why these dictionaries matter



Each pair of braces creates a dictionary. Text before a colon is a field name; the value after it is what the record stores. The brackets around the two records create a list. research_records[0]["route"] first selects item 0 from that list and then selects the "route" field from the chosen dictionary. The two outputs are not averaged or declared correct. They remain attached to route, requested model and input so a later reviewer can see what produced each proposed score.




Methodological check
The two scores are proposed measurements. Neither route establishes that the score matches the intended construct or a defensible human codebook. If local_answer is None, the local route was deliberately skipped in Colab; it is not a model response.

title: Week 2 — When can an LLM label count as a measure?
text:
Sociological and methodological background
Text does not arrive as a variable. Sociologists and political scientists have long moved from documents to data by defining constructs, writing codebooks, training research assistants and adjudicating hard cases. Computational text analysis made parts of this work scalable; crowdworker platforms such as MTurk and Prolific made it easier to distribute judgments beyond expert teams. Those changes lowered cost but did not remove the need to decide what counts as evidence for the construct.
An LLM prompt is therefore not a free-standing instruction. It contains a codebook in compressed form: the label names, inclusion and exclusion rules, examples, output format and sometimes a role or rationale. Stuhler and colleagues call attention to this move from codebook to promptbook. The useful comparison is not “human versus AI” in the abstract, but two complete measurement procedures applied to a stated use.

title: Week 2 — When can an LLM label count as a measure?
section: Synthesis of the current LLM literature
text:
Synthesis of the current LLM literature
Three issues should remain separate. Reliability asks whether reasonable repetitions or prompt formulations agree. Validity asks whether the labels represent the intended construct. Downstream error asks how mistakes affect the estimate or model in which the labels are used. Prompt Stability Score addresses the first. A human-coded validation sample and difficult boundary cases contribute to the second. Confusion counts and design-based corrections address the third. A classifier can have high overall accuracy and still inflate a rare category if its false positives are concentrated in one direction.

comment is the text to classify. codebook is a dictionary mapping each permitted label to its definition. human_label is a separate reference judgment; it is not sent to the model. codebook["UNCLEAR"] uses a key to retrieve one definition and demonstrates how dictionaries differ from lists.




Construct the exact message list used by both routes
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
prompt = (
    "Apply this codebook: " + json.dumps(codebook) +
    "\nReturn only SUPPORT, OPPOSE, or UNCLEAR.\nComment: " + comment
)
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
print(messages[0]["content"])






From codebook to model input



json.dumps(codebook) turns the Python dictionary into readable text that can be placed inside the prompt. The + signs join codebook, instruction and comment. The resulting messages list contains one user message. [0] retrieves the first list item; ["content"] then retrieves that dictionary’s content field.




Make and unpack the OpenRouter call
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
with OpenRouter(api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]) as client:
    hosted_response = client.chat.send(
        model=HOSTED_MODEL, messages=messages, temperature=0,
    )
hosted_choice = hosted_response.choices[0]
hosted_raw = hosted_choice.message.content
print("OpenRouter raw return:", hosted_raw)
hosted_label = hosted_raw.strip().upper()
print("OpenRouter label:", hosted_label)






Hosted label



The inputs are the hosted model, the shared message list and zero temperature. [0] chooses the first returned choice, .message.content retrieves its text, .strip() removes spare whitespace and .upper() standardizes letter case. The final output, hosted_label, remains a string and may still fall outside the codebook.

Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
if IN_COLAB:
    local_response = None
    local_raw = None
    local_label = None
    print("Ollama was not called: Colab cannot reach the local Ollama server.")
else:
    local_response = ollama.chat(think=False, 
        model=LOCAL_MODEL, messages=messages, options={"temperature": 0},
    )
    local_raw = local_response.message.content
    print("Ollama raw return:", local_raw)
    local_label = local_raw.strip().upper()
    print("Ollama label:", local_label)






Local label



if IN_COLAB checks the Boolean created by the setup cell. In Colab, no local request is attempted and the local values become None. Locally, the same messages enter Ollama. Its temperature sits inside an options dictionary and its returned text is found at local_response.message.content. Standardizing case makes the two strings easier to compare; it does not repair a substantively wrong label.




Compare route agreement and human-reference agreement
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
routes_agree = None if local_label is None else hosted_label == local_label
hosted_matches_human = hosted_label == human_label
local_matches_human = None if local_label is None else local_label == human_label
print("Routes agree:", routes_agree)
print("OpenRouter matches human label:", hosted_matches_human)
print("Ollama matches human label:", local_matches_human)

# ONE CHANGE: replace comment with
# "I oppose the rezoning proposal because it will displace tenants."
# Then rerun from the message-construction cell.






Three Boolean outputs



Each == asks whether two strings are equal and returns True or False. The short if ... else ... expressions first check whether Ollama ran. In Colab the local comparisons return None, which means “not run,” not disagreement. routes_agree compares the two models; the other two values compare each model with the independently supplied human reference.




Methodological check
Agreement between the routes is a reproducibility observation. Agreement with one human label is criterion evidence. Neither alone proves that the codebook measures the construct well. If an Ollama comparison prints None, the local route was deliberately skipped in Colab.

Connection to the preceding material
Week 2 began with a construct and a predefined label set. Qualitative analysis often begins less settled. Codes develop, comparisons redirect attention and memos connect passages to emerging ideas. The problem is not only whether a model applies a rule correctly, but how its suggestions reorganize the researcher’s attention.

section: Essential readings and what each contributes
text:
Essential readings and what each contributes


Methods: Timmermans and Tavory (2012), “Theory Construction in Qualitative Research,” Sociological Theory. Read the complete article. It explains abductive analysis: surprising observations become analytically useful through comparison with alternative theoretical accounts. DOI. (Timmermans and Tavory 2012)
Methods and LLMs: Than et al. (2025), “Updating ‘The Future of Coding’,” Sociological Methods & Research. Read the complete article. It provides a researcher–LLM–researcher workflow and an empirical comparison of human and model-assisted coding. DOI. (Than et al. 2025)
Substantive application: Viterna (2006), “Pulled, Pushed, and Persuaded,” American Journal of Sociology. Read the complete article. Viterna uses life histories and event-level comparisons to explain different routes into high-risk mobilization; we use it to see what qualitative analysis must preserve before asking an LLM for themes. DOI. (Viterna 2006)

title: Week 3 — What can an LLM contribute to qualitative interpretation?
text:
Additional readings grouped by purpose

For reflexivity about the model interaction: Ibrahim and Voyer (2026), “Qualitative Research with LLM Chatbots,” Qualitative Research. DOI. (Ibrahim and Voyer 2026)
For a recent empirical implementation: Jack, Cooper and Flower (2026), “Automating the Qualitative Interview?” Methodological Innovations. DOI. (Jack, Cooper, and Flower 2026)

title: Week 3 — What can an LLM contribute to qualitative interpretation?
text:
Sociological and methodological background
Qualitative analysis is not a single request for “the themes.” Researchers read and re-read material, write provisional codes, compare passages and cases, record hunches, search for exceptions and revise the relationship between data and theory. Timmermans and Tavory emphasize abduction: an unexpected observation becomes productive when it is developed against alternative theoretical accounts. A list of frequent topics is therefore not equivalent to an interpretation.
Viterna shows what this looks like in substantive research. Her explanation of women’s routes into Salvadoran guerrilla organizations depends on reconstructing sequences within life histories and comparing different paths into mobilization. The same broad topic can appear in several accounts while doing different explanatory work. That is exactly the kind of difference a decontextualized list of themes can erase.
Our worked corpus consists of short interview excerpts about tenant mutual-aid networks. Each excerpt has an ID, speaker, question, preceding context and text. The research question asks how participants describe the relationship between mutual aid and formal housing organizations. Giving the listener this setup matters: the same sentence could support a different interpretation in a study of friendship, political mobilization or service provision.

title: Week 3 — What can an LLM contribute to qualitative interpretation?
section: Synthesis of the current LLM literature
text:
Synthesis of the current LLM literature
Than and colleagues show that models can contribute useful code suggestions while researchers retain decisions about meaning and iteration. Ibrahim and Voyer ask researchers to document how the chatbot’s categories and conversational affordances enter the analysis. Both point away from one-shot automation. Context windows are large but finite; calls may not preserve cumulative analytic memory; summaries can smooth over contradictions; and a model can cite genuine passages while overstating what they show. The worked exercise therefore asks the model for a provisional suggestion and a source ID, then sends the researcher back to the passage. Viterna gives us the harder standard: can the analysis preserve chronology, comparison across cases and evidence that does not fit the first proposed theme?

title: Week 4 — What part of social experience becomes evidence?
section: Essential readings and what each contributes
text:
Essential readings and what each contributes


Methods: Goodwin (1994), “Professional Vision,” American Anthropologist 96(3): 606–633. Read the complete article. It shows how coding, highlighting and material representations organize what members of a profession see. DOI. (Goodwin 1994)
Methods: Nassauer and Legewie (2021), “Video Data Analysis,” Sociological Methods & Research 50(1): 135–174. Read the complete article. It gives a systematic account of selection, sequencing, transcription and inference when video becomes sociological data. DOI. (Nassauer and Legewie 2021)
Substantive application: Collins (2013), “Entering and Leaving the Tunnel of Violence,” Current Sociology 61(2): 132–151. Read the complete article. Collins uses visual evidence and close sequence analysis to explain confrontation, tension and entrainment. DOI. (Collins 2013)

title: Week 4 — What part of social experience becomes evidence?

Additional readings grouped by purpose

For the technical grounding debate: Bisk et al. (2020), “Experience Grounds Language,” EMNLP. Paper. (Bisk et al. 2020)

title: Week 4 — What part of social experience becomes evidence?
text:
Sociological and methodological background
Simmel’s sociology of the senses and Goffman’s interaction order make perception and situated conduct sociological topics. Goodwin goes further: relevant objects do not simply announce themselves. Practitioners learn to code a field of activity, highlight selected features and use material representations that make a judgment possible. His examples show that seeing is socially organized.
Collins’s theory of violent situations redirects attention from violent people to sequences of interaction. Confrontational tension and fear often inhibit violence; particular configurations allow participants to move through that barrier and sometimes enter a “tunnel” of emotional entrainment. This is a claim about timing and relation. A still image of contact cannot show the full sequence that preceded it.
Our empirical illustration is the Zidane–Materazzi confrontation in the 2006 World Cup final. Broadcast video supplies multiple views and a public chronology, but it does not give direct access to inner intention. The example allows us to distinguish what is visible—the turn, approach and headbutt—from Collins’s situational interpretation and from later biographical accounts.

title: Week 4 — What part of social experience becomes evidence?
section: Synthesis of the current LLM literature
text:
Synthesis of the current LLM literature
Multimodal models can describe frames, transcribe audio and compare moments. They also arrive with pretrained recognition that may identify famous people or retrieve a culturally familiar narrative. That can be useful, but it can contaminate a task designed to inspect only visible conduct. World-model research asks whether models can learn predictive representations of physical environments; sociology asks an additional question: which social experiences, relations and professional categories have been made legible to the model at all?
The defensible workflow constrains the first pass to observable features, preserves time and source, and records later theoretical interpretation separately. We can then deliberately compare a frame-only call, a sequence call and a context-rich call.

title: Week 5 — Can generated media isolate a causal construct?
text:
Sociological and methodological background
Sociologists intervene in several ways. A vignette describes a situation and asks for a judgment; a factorial survey varies several attributes across vignettes; an audit study sends matched applications that differ on a focal signal; a confederate enacts a standardized role in a social setting. The concrete objects differ, but each design depends on controlling which feature changes and what comparison that change licenses.
Wallander’s review matters because generated text does not make this design logic obsolete. An LLM can produce a larger candidate pool, but every candidate still embeds word choice, tone, plausibility and social assumptions. If one paid-leave frame mentions “hard-working families” and another mentions “national productivity,” the conditions differ in more than a short label. Those semantic differences are potential confounds.

title: Week 5 — Can generated media isolate a causal construct?
section: Synthesis of the current LLM literature
text:
Synthesis of the current LLM literature
Recent work shows the value of generation without equating it with treatment readiness. Bai and colleagues generate and test policy messages on human participants. Velez separates an adaptive selection process from the population in which questions are evaluated. Dafoe and colleagues offer a precise standard for our review: non-focal information should be held equivalent across conditions. The LLM is useful upstream, where it can widen the pool. Human pretests and design checks remain necessary downstream.

import time

ROUTE = "openrouter" if IN_COLAB else "ollama"  # Ollama is the local default
shared_facts = (
    "The proposal would create a pathway to permanent legal status for undocumented "
    "immigrants who meet residency and background-check requirements."
)
frame = "rights"
temperature = 0.7
max_tokens = 140






Separate what stays fixed



The facts and frame are separate strings so the exercise can change one while holding the other constant. temperature is a float and maximum_output_tokens is an integer. They are recorded as model-call inputs, not treated as substantive properties of the message.




Construct the prompt with an f-string
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
prompt = (
    f"Write one 70–90 word survey message using a {frame} frame. "
    f"Use only these facts and return only the message:\n\n{shared_facts}"
)
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
print(prompt)






How the f-string works



The leading f allows values inside braces to be inserted into a string. {frame} and {facts} are replaced by their current values. The output is one complete prompt; printing it is how we check that the intended frame changed and the factual material did not.




Make one timed call and preserve route-specific metadata
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
started = time.perf_counter()
if ROUTE == "openrouter":
    with OpenRouter(api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]) as client:
        response = client.chat.send(
            model=HOSTED_MODEL, messages=messages,
            temperature=temperature, max_tokens=max_tokens,
        )
    raw_output = response.choices[0].message.content
    input_tokens = getattr(response.usage, "prompt_tokens", None)
    output_tokens = getattr(response.usage, "completion_tokens", None)
else:
    response = ollama.chat(think=False, 
        model=LOCAL_MODEL, messages=messages,
        options={"temperature": temperature, "num_predict": max_tokens},
    )
    raw_output = response.message.content
    input_tokens = response.prompt_eval_count
    output_tokens = response.eval_count
latency_seconds = round(time.perf_counter() - started, 2)

print("Raw candidate:", raw_output.strip())
print("Input tokens:", input_tokens)
print("Output tokens:", output_tokens)
print("Latency seconds:", latency_seconds)






Call inputs and observed outputs



time.perf_counter() records a clock value before and after the call; subtraction gives elapsed seconds. The selected branch supplies model, messages, temperature and output limit. It then retrieves the candidate text and, where available, token-use metadata. Latency and token counts describe this run, not the candidate’s validity.

Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.

    "route": ROUTE,
    "frame": frame,
    "shared_facts": shared_facts,
    "temperature": temperature,
    "max_tokens": max_tokens,
    "raw_output": raw_output.strip(),

print(candidate_record)

The candidate record



The dictionary stores the changing frame, fixed facts, route, model, settings, elapsed time and generated text together. This is the output needed for the later causal-design review. The named change asks for a second candidate; comparison should isolate intended framing from other semantic differences.




Methodological check
Holding the prompt variables fixed does not guarantee that the generated messages differ only in framing. Compare facts, certainty, tone, length and implied beneficiaries before treating them as experimental stimuli.

title: Week 6 — What changes when a model starts asking the questions?
text:
Sociological and methodological background
Interviews have never been neutral containers into which respondents deposit attitudes. Merton and Kendall’s focused interview sought detailed responses to a known situation while allowing unanticipated meanings to emerge. Later feminist and reflexive work made power, reciprocity and the interviewer’s social position part of the method. Standardized survey interviewing pursued comparability; CAPI moved administration onto an interviewer’s computer; CASI allowed self-administration; audio-CASI added recorded speech for accessibility and privacy. These modes change what respondents hear, disclose and understand.
Rivera’s study makes the evidentiary stakes concrete. Interviewers described cultural fit, while observation showed how evaluators converted shared tastes and experiences into judgments about candidates. The two sources do not simply duplicate one another. An adaptive interviewer might elicit a specific evaluative episode, but a leading probe could also supply the very explanation the study is meant to discover.
An LLM interviewer redistributes familiar decisions. A protocol can set topic boundaries and fixed questions. After an answer, a model can select a prepared follow-up or compose a new one. The second option can pursue specificity, but it can also lead, presuppose a cause, repeat itself or create incomparable paths across participants.

title: Week 6 — What changes when a model starts asking the questions?
section: Synthesis of the current LLM literature
text:
Synthesis of the current LLM literature
Geiecke and Jaravel use text and voice, so their system includes speech-to-text before the language model and text-to-speech after it. Jack and colleagues use a web chatbot built around Gemini Flash 1.5 and study both the interview data and researchers’ experience of the system. These implementations make privacy, retention and data ownership design questions: which service receives audio, where transcripts are stored, and whether data are reused. A local stack can reduce external transfer, but it demands hardware, model files, maintenance and usually slower inference.
The evaluation target also matters. Completion rate and conversational fluency do not establish qualitative richness. A controlled design can compare fixed questions, dynamic probing and member checking, but the concepts must be defined: a dynamic prober generates a follow-up from the answer; a member checker asks whether the interviewer’s understanding is accurate. In the worked example, the check is deliberately substantive: does the follow-up ask an evaluator to describe a concrete hiring decision, or does it prematurely name “cultural fit” as the cause?

Choose a route and construct the opening interview history
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
ROUTE = "openrouter" if IN_COLAB else "ollama"  # Ollama is the local default
interview_messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": (
        "Conduct a sociological interview. Ask one short follow-up about a concrete "
        "episode. Do not suggest a cause or put words in the participant's mouth."
    )},
    {"role": "user", "content": (
        "Participant: I spoke after the professor invited me to respond."
    )},
]
print(interview_messages)






Conversation as ordered state



history is a list of dictionaries in chronological order. Roles say whether an item is an interviewing instruction or participant speech. This complete list becomes the input to the first call. Reordering or omitting an item would change what the model can use.




Make the first call through the selected route
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
if ROUTE == "openrouter":
    with OpenRouter(api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]) as client:
        first_response = client.chat.send(
            model=HOSTED_MODEL, messages=interview_messages, temperature=0,
        )
    first_raw = first_response.choices[0].message.content
else:
    first_response = ollama.chat(think=False, 
        model=LOCAL_MODEL, messages=interview_messages,
        options={"temperature": 0},
    )
    first_raw = first_response.message.content
print("First raw return:", first_raw)
first_probe = first_raw.strip()
print("First probe:", first_probe)






The first adaptive probe



The if/else branch sends the same history through the chosen route. Both branches store returned text in probe_one. That string is the model’s proposed next interviewer turn; the later check asks whether it follows the participant’s answer without supplying a cause.




Append the realized probe and a second participant answer
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
interview_messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": first_probe})
second_answer = "Participant: I felt safer because she made room for me to speak."
interview_messages.append({"role": "user", "content": second_answer})
print("Messages before second call:", len(interview_messages))
print(interview_messages)






What append changes



.append(...) mutates the existing list by adding one dictionary at its end. The first append records what the model asked; the second records the participant’s next answer. Printing the history shows the new ordered input that the second call will receive.




Make the second call with the expanded history
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
if ROUTE == "openrouter":
    with OpenRouter(api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]) as client:
        second_response = client.chat.send(
            model=HOSTED_MODEL, messages=interview_messages, temperature=0,
        )
    second_raw = second_response.choices[0].message.content
else:
    second_response = ollama.chat(think=False, 
        model=LOCAL_MODEL, messages=interview_messages,
        options={"temperature": 0},
    )
    second_raw = second_response.message.content
print("Second raw return:", second_raw)
second_probe = second_raw.strip()
print("Second probe:", second_probe)

# ONE CHANGE: replace second_answer with
# "Participant: I spoke when there was a pause." and rerun from append onward.






Why the second call differs



The call syntax is unchanged, but history now contains two additional turns. The returned probe_two can therefore respond to the new answer. Comparing the two probes checks continuity, leading language and repetition; it does not by itself establish interview quality.




Methodological check
Inspect whether each probe follows the participant’s words, asks for a concrete episode, avoids repetition and does not name a cause in advance.

title: Week 7 — Whose attitudes do synthetic respondents represent?
text:
Sociological and methodological background
Survey inference depends on more than asking a question. Probability sampling links observed respondents to a target population; questionnaire design shapes the answers; total survey error directs attention to coverage, sampling, nonresponse, measurement and processing. Simulmatics provides an instructive prehistory: in 1960 the company used survey segments and computational models to advise the Kennedy campaign. The ambition to model an electorate is older than LLMs, as are the problems created by missing and poorly measured groups.
Public opinion theory adds another caution. Zaller treats a survey response as something assembled at the time from accessible considerations, not a stable value stored unchanged in a person. A demographic persona such as “a 42-year-old Black woman in Georgia” therefore does not reproduce the experiences, networks and information environment through which a human answer is formed.
Igarashi, Kano and Miwa turn this general warning into an empirical comparison. Human respondents and GPT-4 judge the same experimentally varied scenarios of unequal treatment. This lets us ask two separate questions: whether the model gives similar average judgments, and whether it responds to changes in the scenario in the same way as people do. Similarity on one does not guarantee similarity on the other.

title: Week 7 — Whose attitudes do synthetic respondents represent?
section: Synthesis of the current LLM literature
text:
Synthesis of the current LLM literature
The literature now contains several distinct designs. A model can predict an aggregate distribution, answer once per persona, predict a held-out answer for a real respondent, or act through an interview-grounded record. These are not interchangeable. Matching the modal response does not recover the distribution; matching the distribution does not recover individual pairings; aggregate resemblance can coexist with flattened subgroup heterogeneity. Igarashi and colleagues add another target: responsiveness to an experimental treatment. Validation must name which of these targets matters before calculating a score.

text:
Today’s routine: One deidentified profile → one structured prediction → three schema checks → held-out comparison.
Python introduced: JSON Schema, required fields, numeric lists, len(...), sum(...) and Boolean checks.
Your change: change only age_group, rerun and compare the probability lists.



Load the course settings and SDKs
Run the notebook’s Prepare the notebook environment cell first. It installs missing SDKs in Colab, checks the local uv environment, adds the repository root to Python’s import path and sets IN_COLAB. Colab uses OpenRouter because it cannot reach the Ollama server on your computer.
This next cell reads the two centrally recorded model names and asks for the hosted key without displaying it. Treat the key entry as setup; never include it in the recording.
import json
import os
from getpass import getpass
from pathlib import Path

try:
    import ollama
    from openrouter import OpenRouter
except ModuleNotFoundError as error:
    raise ModuleNotFoundError(
        "A course SDK is missing. Open a terminal in the complete GenAI_Soc2026 "
        "folder, run 'uv sync --frozen', then run this task with 'uv run python'."
    ) from error

ROOT = Path.cwd()
while not (ROOT / "config" / "course_models.json").exists() and ROOT != ROOT.parent:
    ROOT = ROOT.parent

if not (ROOT / "config" / "course_models.json").exists():
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "The complete GenAI_Soc2026 repository could not be found. A task or "
        "notebook downloaded by itself is not enough for local work. Open a terminal "
        "in the complete course folder and run this file from there."
    )

config = json.loads((ROOT / "config" / "course_models.json").read_text())
HOSTED_MODEL = config["hosted"]["model"]
LOCAL_MODEL = config["local"]["model"]

if not os.getenv("OPENROUTER_API_KEY"):
    os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"] = getpass("OpenRouter course key (hidden): ")

print("Hosted model:", HOSTED_MODEL)
print("Local model:", LOCAL_MODEL)






Read this setup cell



Input: installed Python packages, config/course_models.json, and—if it is not already set—the hidden OpenRouter key. Operations: import makes an installed tool available; Path.cwd() gives Python the current folder; the while block walks upward until it finds the course configuration; json.loads(...) turns the file’s JSON text into a dictionary; square brackets retrieve the two model names. Output: HOSTED_MODEL and LOCAL_MODEL are strings. getpass(...) accepts the key without echoing it. The folder-search code is supplied setup and is not assessed.




Choose a route and store one deidentified profile and survey item
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
ROUTE = "openrouter" if IN_COLAB else "ollama"  # Ollama is the local default
profile = {
    "age_group": "30–44",
    "education": "bachelor's degree",
    "region": "South",
    "party_identification": "independent",
}
question = (
    "On a scale from 1 (very liberal) to 7 (very conservative), "
    "where would you place yourself?"
)
held_out_human_answer = 4
print(profile)
print(question)






Profile, question and held-out answer



profile is a dictionary containing public-use teaching attributes; survey_item is the exact question string. held_out_human_answer is stored separately and is not included in the prompt. This separation prevents the model from seeing the answer it is meant to predict.




Define the exact output structure
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "predicted_category": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 7},
        "probabilities": {
            "type": "array", "items": {"type": "number"},
            "minItems": 7, "maxItems": 7,
        },
    },
    "required": ["predicted_category", "probabilities"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}
prompt = (
    "Predict this deidentified respondent's answer. Return seven probabilities in "
    "order from 1 to 7. Profile: " + json.dumps(profile) + " Item: " + question
)
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]






Reading the JSON Schema



The schema requires an integer category from 1 to 7 and a seven-number probability list. required says both fields must appear; additionalProperties: False prohibits extra fields. These rules concern readable structure and numeric bounds, not whether the prediction represents people well.




Make the selected structured-output call
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
if ROUTE == "openrouter":
    with OpenRouter(api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]) as client:
        response = client.chat.send(
            model=HOSTED_MODEL, messages=messages, temperature=0,
            response_format={"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {
                "name": "polviews_prediction", "strict": True, "schema": schema,
            }},
        )
    raw_output = response.choices[0].message.content
else:
    response = ollama.chat(think=False, 
        model=LOCAL_MODEL, messages=messages, format=schema,
        options={"temperature": 0},
    )
    raw_output = response.message.content
print("Raw JSON text:", raw_output)






Two ways to request the same structure



The prompt joins the profile and exact item into one message. OpenRouter places the schema in response_format; Ollama receives it through format. Both branches preserve the returned JSON text in raw_json before any field is extracted.




Parse, check structure and only then compare with the held-out answer
Run this block, print its output and explain what enters and leaves the operation. The next block uses the value created here.
prediction = json.loads(raw_output)
probabilities = prediction["probabilities"]
seven_values = len(probabilities) == 7
sum_is_close = abs(sum(probabilities) - 1.0) < 0.02
matches_human = prediction["predicted_category"] == held_out_human_answer
print("Predicted category:", prediction["predicted_category"])
print("Seven probabilities:", seven_values)
print("Sum close to one:", sum_is_close)
print("Held-out human answer:", held_out_human_answer)
print("Exact match:", matches_human)

# ONE CHANGE: change age_group to "18–29" and rerun.






Structure check versus evidence check



Parsing creates a dictionary. len(probabilities) counts entries and sum(probabilities) adds them; comparisons produce Booleans checking seven values, an approximate total of one and values between zero and one. Only after those mechanical checks is predicted_category compared with the held-out human answer. One match is not population validation.




Methodological check
A valid schema means Python can retrieve the required fields. One exact match does not establish individual accuracy, group fidelity or population representation.

title: Week 8 — Can LLMs recover opinions we did not observe?
text:
Sociological and methodological background
Social scientists already estimate quantities they do not observe directly. Lax and Phillips combine actual survey responses, a multilevel model and census population counts to estimate state opinion, then use those estimates to study policy responsiveness. Their evidence chain matters: observed answers and known population margins constrain the estimate, validation is explicit, and the estimated opinion serves a substantive analysis rather than becoming an end in itself.
An LLM prediction changes this chain. Kim and Lee train on questions, respondents’ other answers and survey years to study three tasks: imputing a missing answer, retrodicting an item not asked in a particular wave and predicting an opinion never asked in the survey. These tasks expose the model to different amounts of relevant evidence and therefore warrant different claims.

title: Week 8 — Can LLMs recover opinions we did not observe?
section: Synthesis of the current LLM literature
text:
Synthesis of the current LLM literature
Xie and colleagues evaluate whether generated datasets preserve distributions, bivariate associations, multivariate relationships, life-event sequences and links between sequences and covariates. Their results show why “the synthetic data look realistic” is too vague. A model can approximate a marginal distribution while compressing subgroup variation or changing relationships among variables. Kim and Lee likewise separate individual- and aggregate-level performance. Ashokkumar and colleagues extend prediction to experimental findings, but that is a different target again.
The coding example keeps the distinction visible. Five real teaching profiles are passed through OpenRouter and Ollama. The human answer is withheld from each prompt, every raw return is saved, and individual exact matches are calculated separately from the aggregate mean. Five records are not a validation study; they are enough to learn how a repeated model routine works and why the metric must match the claim.

title: Week 8 Python — Repeat predictions and compare routes
text:
Today’s routine: Five deidentified profiles → the same request through OpenRouter and Ollama → one saved record per case and route → individual and aggregate comparisons.
Python introduced: the first for loop around a model call, empty lists, loop variables, .append(...), counters and division.
Your change: change only the education field for case p02, rerun and compare the two kinds of result.



Load the settings and start with five records
Run the notebook setup cell first. It installs missing packages in Colab, locates the repository locally and reads the centrally recorded model names. The setup code is supplied and is not the assessed Python for this week.
profiles = [
    {"id": "p01", "age_group": "18–29", "education": "some college",
     "region": "Northeast", "party": "Democrat", "human_answer": 2},
    {"id": "p02", "age_group": "30–44", "education": "bachelor's",
     "region": "South", "party": "Independent", "human_answer": 4},
    # Three further records are supplied in the notebook.
]

question = "Place yourself from 1 (very liberal) to 7 (very conservative)."
print("Number of profiles:", len(profiles))






Read the input before running it



profiles is a list. Each item is a dictionary representing one deidentified case. human_answer is retained for the later comparison but must be removed from the dictionary sent to the model. question is a string. len(profiles) returns the integer number of cases.




Create two empty result lists
hosted_results = []
local_results = []

print(hosted_results)
print(local_results)






Input and output



There is no data input yet. Each pair of square brackets creates an empty list. After each model call, .append(...) will add one result dictionary. Keeping two lists means we do not lose which route produced a prediction.




Follow one trip through the loop
for profile in profiles:
    public_profile = {
        "age_group": profile["age_group"],
        "education": profile["education"],
        "region": profile["region"],
        "party": profile["party"],
    }

    prompt = (
        "Predict the survey answer. Profile: "
        + json.dumps(public_profile)
        + " Item: "
        + question
    )
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]






What the loop changes



On the first pass, profile means profiles[0]; on the second, it means profiles[1]. public_profile copies only the fields the model may see, so human_answer is absent. json.dumps(...) turns that dictionary into text. The output of this block is one messages list ready for a model call.




Make both calls and keep the raw text
    with OpenRouter(api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]) as client:
        hosted_response = client.chat.send(
            model=HOSTED_MODEL,
            messages=messages,
            temperature=0,
            response_format={
                "type": "json_schema",
                "json_schema": {
                    "name": "opinion_prediction",
                    "strict": True,
                    "schema": schema,
                },
            },
        )
    hosted_raw = hosted_response.choices[0].message.content

    local_response = ollama.chat(think=False,
        model=LOCAL_MODEL,
        messages=messages,
        format=schema,
        options={"temperature": 0},
    )
    local_raw = local_response.message.content

    print(profile["id"], "hosted:", hosted_raw, "local:", local_raw)






Two routes, the same research input



Both calls receive the same messages list and a schema requiring an answer from 1 to 7. OpenRouter sends the request to the hosted model; Ollama sends it to the local model already running on the computer. hosted_raw and local_raw are strings. Printing them before parsing makes the original returns visible.




Parse and append one record to each list
    hosted_prediction = json.loads(hosted_raw)["predicted_category"]
    local_prediction = json.loads(local_raw)["predicted_category"]

    hosted_results.append({
        "id": profile["id"],
        "prediction": hosted_prediction,
        "human": profile["human_answer"],
    })
    local_results.append({
        "id": profile["id"],
        "prediction": local_prediction,
        "human": profile["human_answer"],
    })






What .append(...) does



json.loads(...) turns each JSON string into a dictionary; square brackets retrieve its predicted category. Each .append(...) adds one new dictionary to the end of a result list. After five passes through the loop, each list contains five records.




Count exact matches, then compare the aggregate means
hosted_matches = 0
for record in hosted_results:
    if record["prediction"] == record["human"]:
        hosted_matches = hosted_matches + 1

human_total = 0
hosted_total = 0
for record in hosted_results:
    human_total = human_total + record["human"]
    hosted_total = hosted_total + record["prediction"]

human_mean = human_total / len(hosted_results)
hosted_mean = hosted_total / len(hosted_results)

print("Hosted exact matches:", hosted_matches)
print("Human mean:", human_mean)
print("Hosted mean:", hosted_mean)






These are different checks



The first loop asks whether the prediction and human answer match case by case. The second adds the values before dividing by the number of records. A close mean can coexist with poor individual prediction because over-predictions and under-predictions can cancel. The notebook repeats both calculations for the local route.




Methodological check
Five teaching cases cannot establish individual accuracy, subgroup fidelity or population validity. The exercise demonstrates how to preserve matched records and why a claim about an aggregate requires a different check from a claim about people.
